title: Architecture standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance & ADRs (Addendum)
author: Alex Rivera
content:
Overview

This document consolidates our canonical architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance targets, and a set of recent decision records (ADRs). It is an addendum to the master Architecture Standards and is intended for service owners, platform engineers, and reviewers responsible for onboarding new services or changing runtime behavior.

Scope
- Applies to all services that are part of Redwood Inference: public APIs (hosted), internal microservices, model-serving runtime components, and infra IaC modules.
- Excludes one-off research notebooks and personal experiments (those belong in Drive).

Key contacts and ownership
- Standards owner: engineering-architecture (primary contact: Alex Rivera)
- Reviewers: Priya Menon (platform), Jordan Kim (runtime), Liam O'Connor (observability)

1) API Standards
Purpose: Ensure consistent, observable, and maintainable external and internal APIs.

Design principles
- External-facing APIs (console + public SDKs): REST/JSON or well-documented GraphQL for complex read queries. Provide OpenAPI v3 spec for all REST APIs.
- Internal/high-throughput RPCs: gRPC with proto3 for binary efficiency and strong typing.
- Backwards compatibility: follow semver on API surface. Major version bump required for breaking changes; minor/patch for non-breaking additions/bug fixes.
- Field naming: snake_case for backend JSON payloads. SDKs may map to idiomatic casing per language (camelCase for JavaScript).
- Idempotency & retries: support idempotency_token for any write operation. Document retry semantics and safe idempotency windows.

Contract & versioning
- Each API must publish: OpenAPI/Proto file, example requests/responses, and a compatibility matrix.
- Header conventions: X-Request-Id (uuid), X-Account-Id, X-Env (prod/staging). Always propagate Traceparent for tracing.

Timeouts and Throttling
- Public request timeout: client-facing 30s default; streaming endpoints allowed longer but must document expected session TTL.
- Internal RPC timeouts: default 5s for control-plane calls, 60s for long-running inference orchestration steps that aggregate results.
- Rate limiting: per-account token buckets; include Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* headers.

Example OpenAPI snippet (simplified):

```yaml
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Redwood Inference Public API
  version: 2026-03-01
paths:
  /v1/generate:
    post:
      summary: Generate text for a model
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/GenerateRequest'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: successful response
components:
  schemas:
    GenerateRequest:
      type: object
      properties:
        model:
          type: string
        prompt:
          type: string
        max_tokens:
          type: integer
```

2) Coding Standards
Goal: readable, testable, and reviewable code across services.

Language guidance
- Runtime (latency-sensitive): Go 1.21+ for statically typed, low-latency services.
- Orchestration & infra tools: Python 3.11+ for rapid iteration and existing ecosystem.
- Console and customer-facing UI: TypeScript (strict mode) + React.

Quality controls
- Linting: golangci-lint (Go), flake8 + black (Python), eslint + prettier (TS).
- Testing: unit tests with >=80% coverage target for core service logic; integration tests gated on CI.
- CI gates: build, lint, unit tests, basic integration smoke tests, and SCA (software composition analysis) before merge to main.
- PR size policy: prefer PRs <400 LOC; >1000 LOC require architecture signoff.
- Code review SLA: reviewers should respond within 24 business hours for non-urgent PRs.

Security
- Secrets must not be in repo; use KMS-backed secrets manager (see infra standards).
- Static analysis: SAST on every main branch merge; remediate high severity within 3 business days.

3) Infrastructure Standards (IaC, networking, secrets)
IaC & environments
- Terraform (>=1.4) with shared modules living in infra-modules repo. Reuse modules for VPC, IAM roles, GPU pool, and monitoring.
- Environments: prod, staging, dev. Each environment must be isolated accounts/projects with RBAC controls.

Naming & tagging
- Resource names: <team>-<service>-<env>-<component> (kebab-case).
- Required tags: owner, cost_center, env, sla_tier.

Networking & security
- Private subnets for model-serving GPU pools. Public endpoints must be fronted by the API edge with WAF.
- VPC peering and PrivateLink for private deployments. Document egress rules and approved third-party endpoints.

Secrets & keys
- KMS for keys; HSM for customer-managed keys in Private deployments. Rotate keys annually or on any suspected compromise.

4) Model-Serving Standards
This section prescribes how models are onboarded, versioned, and served.

Model manifest (required for onboarding)
- Each model must include a model_manifest.yaml containing: model_id, architecture, parameters, sequence_length_limits, quantization_profile, recommended_batching, memory_requirements, fallback_model_id.

Quantization & compatibility
- Quantization profiles are stored in the quantization-profiles directory and referenced by manifest. Profiles must include accuracy delta targets and hardware compatibility.

Rollouts & traffic shaping
- Canary policy: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% over a minimum 24-hour window with health checks at each step.
- Automatic rollback: if p95 latency increases >30% or error rate >0.5% during rollout step, abort and roll back.

Batching, KV cache, and routing
- Batcher configs: specify target_latency_ms and target_batch_size. Default target_latency_ms = 30ms for interactive routes.
- KV cache TTL: per-model default 1 hour for embedding caches; per-inference prefix caches follow per-route policy.
- Smart routing: models tagged with cost_tier and latency_profile; routing policy evaluates latency SLO, cost preference, and region for decision.

5) Observability Standards
Metrics
- Use OpenTelemetry metrics. All services must export: request_count, request_latency_ms (histogram), error_count, cpu_usage, memory_usage, queue_depth.
- Naming convention: service.<service_name>.<metric> (e.g., service.runtime-batcher.request_latency_ms).

Tracing & logs
- Traces: instrument entry + important downstream calls; propagate trace context.
- Sampling: default adaptive sampling for high-volume paths; 100% sampling for debugging builds.
- Logs: structured JSON with fields: timestamp, level, service, trace_id, request_id, account_id, message. Log retention: 90 days standard; extended retention for security/compliance on request.

Dashboards & alerts
- Dashboards: each service must have a Per-Route Perf dashboard (P50/P95/P99, error rate, throughput, token cost breakdown).
- Alerting thresholds: see Performance SLO table below. Alerts must include runbook links.

Runbooks & oncall
- Every alert must map to a runbook stored under eng-platform/runbooks. Runbook must define oncall steps, mitigation, rollback, and post-incident tags.

6) Performance Standards & SLOs
We define service-level SLOs for the most common interaction patterns: small prompt (<=128 tokens), medium (<=1024), long (>1024). SLOs assume production-tier dedicated capacity unless noted.

| Route type | p50 latency | p95 latency | error rate SLO | Notes |
|-----------|------------:|-----------:|---------------:|------|
| generate (interactive, small) | <= 20 ms/token | <= 100 ms/token | <= 0.2% | prefer batched execution with target_latency_ms=30ms |
| generate (medium) | <= 35 ms/token | <= 180 ms/token | <= 0.5% | ensure KV prefix caching for repeated prompts |
| batch-embed | <= 5 ms/item | <= 30 ms/item | <= 0.1% | higher throughput priorities, allow asynchronous workers |

Operational targets
- CPU/GPU utilization: keep sustained GPU utilization between 50-80% to balance latency and throughput.
- Memory slack: maintain >10% free memory headroom on GPUs to avoid OOM during bursts.
- Cost targets: per-model cost-per-token budgets are defined in pricing-and-packaging and tracked in console; platform teams provide optimization suggestions when budgets exceed 20% of target.

7) Decision Records (ADRs) — recent and canonical
ADR-2025-11: Use gRPC + proto3 for internal high-throughput RPCs
- Decision: internal service-to-service comms will default to gRPC with proto3.
- Rationale: binary serialization reduces overhead for model-routing and kv-cache RPCs; built-in deadlines and streaming support.
- Consequences: all new internal APIs must publish .proto and provide language bindings.

ADR-2026-01: Centralized Quantization Profiles + Per-model Manifest
- Decision: keep quantization profiles centrally versioned and reference them from model manifests.
- Rationale: central profiles enable reproducible accuracy/perf tradeoffs and consistent rollout behavior.
- Consequences: model onboarding requires a compatibility test run; CI will reject manifests referencing unapproved profiles.

ADR-2026-02: API Versioning Strategy
- Decision: follow path-based versioning (/v1/, /v2/) with semantic versioned metadata in headers for client-driven failover.
- Rationale: path-based versioning keeps routing and logging simpler and enables canarying of API surfaces.

8) Adoption & Enforcement
- New service onboarding checklist (required before accepting traffic):
  1. Publish OpenAPI/proto and model_manifest (if applicable).
  2. Add metrics and tracing points per observability checklist.
  3. Provide SLO targets in service metadata and a short runbook.
  4. CI pipeline configured (lint, tests, SCA, infra plan).
  5. Security review for sensitive data handling.

- Standards audit: a quarterly architecture review will evaluate compliance and publish a short report to the architecture-and-standards space. Non-compliant services will be given a remediation plan with owner and timeline.

9) Change process & ADR submission
- To propose a standards change, open an ADR PR in the architecture repo. ADRs must include: decision summary, alternatives considered, benchmarks or perf impact, rollout plan, and owners.
- ADR acceptance: reviewers include architecture lead and two domain experts. Accepted ADRs are assigned an ADR id and added to the canonical ADR index.

Appendix: Example model_manifest.yaml (minimal)

```yaml
model_id: redwood/forrest-v1
architecture: transformer
parameters: 8B
sequence_length_limits:
  min: 1
  max: 8192
quantization_profile: q4_0
recommended_batching:
  target_latency_ms: 30
  max_batch_size: 64
fallback_model_id: redwood/forrest-lite-v1
```
